IGCSE Physics - Radioactivity (1-8)

Question 1 (0625/41_Summer_2017_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) A radioactive source is tested over a number of hours with a radiation detector. The readings are shown in Table 11.1.

Use the readings to suggest a value for the background count rate during the test, and to determine the half-life of the sample. [4]

(b) Hydrogen-3 (tritium) has one proton and two neutrons. The nucleon number of tritium is three. It decays by emitting a β-particle. Complete the nuclide equation to show this decay. The symbol X represents the nuclide produced by this decay. [3]

...H → ...X + ...β

(c) The arrows in Fig. 11.1 show the paths of three α-particles moving towards gold nuclei in a thin foil. On Fig. 11.1, complete the paths of the three α-particles. [3]

(a) The readings level off at an average of around 19-20 counts/s; this is the background count rate. The initial count rate is 324 counts/s. After subtracting the background, the initial sample rate is approx 304 counts/s. After one half-life, the rate would be 152 counts/s. Adding the background, this is 172 counts/s. This does not align perfectly with the table, however, using the mark scheme's logic of halving the corrected reading (324-20=304; 304/2=152) and adding background back (152+20=172) shows the half-life is approximately 1.0 hour.

(b) The completed equation is: 31H → 32He + 0-1β (where X is Helium, He).

(c) The alpha particle heading directly for a nucleus is repelled and deflected back to the left. The one passing close by is deflected on a curved path away from the nucleus. The one passing far away continues undeflected.

Question 2 (0625/42_Summer_2017_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) The arrows in Fig. 11.1 represent the paths of three α-particles moving towards gold nuclei in a thin foil. The gold nuclei are shown as shaded circles. On Fig. 11.1, complete the paths of the three α-particles. [3]

(b) Fig. 11.2 shows a geologist holding a radiation detector near a rock. She holds the detector in a fixed position and records the readings shown in Table 11.1. Explain the changes in the detector readings. [2]

(c) A technician is handling a solid radioactive sample that emits α-particles and β-particles. The technician wears thick rubber gloves. Explain why this may provide some protection from the radiation, but it is not sufficient protection. [2]

(a) The path of the alpha particle that is aimed directly at the nucleus will be deflected at a large angle to the left. The path of the alpha particle passing close to the nucleus will be deflected on a downward curve. The path of the alpha particle passing far from the nucleus will be undeflected.

(b) The readings fluctuate because radioactive decay is a random process. The detector is measuring the background radiation from sources like the rock, which varies naturally.

(c) The thick gloves will stop the α-particles as they have low penetrating power, providing some protection. However, the gloves are not sufficient protection because the more penetrating β-particles can pass through and reach the technician's skin or other body parts.

Question 3 (0625/43_Summer_2017_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) Fig. 11.1 shows equipment that is used to investigate the effect of a magnetic field on the path of a beam of γ-rays.

(i) Suggest the purpose of the two lead plates. [1]

(ii) A magnetic field, directed into the page, is set up in the shaded region. State and explain what happens to the reading of the detector. [3]

(b) State the relative ionising effects of α-particles, β-particles and γ-rays. Suggest an explanation for the differences. [3]

(a)(i) The lead plates are used to absorb stray radiation and produce a narrow beam (collimate) of γ-rays.

(a)(ii) The reading of the detector shows no change. This is because γ-rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation and have no charge, so they are not deflected by a magnetic field.

(b) Ionising effect: α-particles > β-particles > γ-rays. The difference is due to variations in their properties. Alpha particles are the most ionising because they have the largest charge (+2e) and mass, and a lower speed, causing more frequent and intense interactions with atoms over a shorter distance.

Question 4 (0625/43_Winter_2017_Q10) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) State the nature of γ-rays. [1]

(b) A nucleus of technetium-99 emits only a γ-ray. State any effect of this on (i) the proton number of the nucleus, (ii) the nucleon number of the nucleus. [2]

(c) In a laboratory a radiation detector displays a count rate of 16 counts/minute due to background radiation.

(i) State what is meant by background radiation. [1]

(ii) A sample of a radioactive isotope is placed near to the radiation detector and a count rate of 112 counts/minute is recorded. After 18 hours, the count rate recorded is 28 counts/minute. Determine the half-life of this isotope. [3]

(d) Radioactive isotopes are stored in thick lead containers. State two precautions to be taken when radioactive isotopes are used. [2]

(a) γ-rays are high-energy, high-frequency electromagnetic waves.

(b) (i) There is no change in the proton number. (ii) There is no change in the nucleon number.

(c)(i) Background radiation is the low-level ionising radiation that is always present in the environment from natural and man-made sources.

(c)(ii) Corrected initial count rate = 112 - 16 = 96. Corrected final count rate = 28 - 16 = 12. The count rate has dropped from 96 to 12, which is a factor of 8 (96 → 48 → 24 → 12). This represents 3 half-lives. Total time is 18 hours, so the half-life is 18 / 3 = 6.0 hours.

(d) Two precautions are: 1. Handle with tongs to increase distance. 2. Limit exposure time.

Question 5 (0625/41_Winter_2017_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

The radioactive isotope carbon-14 emits β-particles as it decays.

(a) The decay of carbon-14 produces an isotope of nitrogen (N).

(i) State the nature of a β-particle and state where it is produced. [2]

(ii) Complete the nuclide equation for the radioactive decay of carbon-14. [2]

(b) The half-life of carbon-14 is 5700 years. Explain what is meant by the term half-life. [1]

(c) A workman operates a machine that uses β-particles to determine the level of liquid in a plastic water bottle that is being filled. Suggest why (i) α-particles are not suitable for the same purpose, (ii) γ-rays are not suitable for the same purpose. [2]

(a)(i) A β-particle is a high-speed electron that is produced in and emitted from the nucleus when a neutron decays into a proton and an electron.

(a)(ii) The completed equation is: 146C → 147N + 0-1β.

(b) Half-life is the average time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei in a sample to halve (or for the activity/count rate to halve).

(c)(i) α-particles have very low penetrating power and would be stopped (absorbed) by the plastic bottle itself.

(c)(ii) γ-rays are very highly penetrating and would pass through both the bottle and the liquid with little absorption, so there would be no significant change in the detector reading.

Question 6 (0625/42_Winter_2017_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

The radioactive isotope bismuth-210 (210Bi) decays by β-particle emission to an isotope of polonium (Po).

(a) Complete the nuclide equation that represents this decay. [3]

21083Bi → ...Po + ...β

(b) A radiation detector is placed on a bench in a laboratory where there are no artificial sources of radiation. The detector is switched on. In seven one-minute periods, the detector displays these readings: 24, 22, 25, 25, 21, 20, 24.

(i) Explain why, in the absence of any artificial source, there are readings on the detector. Suggest one origin of this effect. [2]

(ii) Explain why the readings obtained are not all the same. [1]

(iii) The half-life of bismuth-210 is 5.0 days. A sample of bismuth-210 is brought close to the detector and in one minute, the reading displayed is 487. The equipment is left in the same place for exactly 10 days. Predict the reading in a one-minute period at the end of this time. [3]

(a) The equation is: 21083Bi → 21084Po + 0-1β.

(b)(i) The detector shows readings because of background radiation which is always present in the environment. One origin is rocks in the Earth's crust (or cosmic rays).

(b)(ii) The readings vary because radioactive decay is a random process.

(b)(iii) The average background count is about 23 counts/min. The initial sample count rate is 487 - 23 = 464 counts/min. 10 days is two half-lives (10 / 5 = 2). After 10 days, the sample count rate will be 464 / 4 = 116 counts/min. The final detector reading will be the sample rate plus the background rate: 116 + 23 = 139 counts/min.

Question 7 (0625/41_Summer_2018_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

Radon-222 is radioactive. It can be represented as 22286Rn.

(a) For a neutral atom of radon-222, state 1. the number of protons, 2. the number of neutrons, 3. the number of electrons. [3]

(b) A radon-222 nucleus decays by α-particle emission to a polonium (Po) nucleus. Complete the equation for the decay of radon-222. [2]

22286Rn → ...Po + ...α

(c) Radon-222 has a half-life of 3.8 days. At a certain time, a sample contains 6.4 × 106 radon nuclei. Calculate the number of α-particles emitted by the radon nuclei in the following 7.6 days. [3]

(a) 1. number of protons = 86. 2. number of neutrons = 222 - 86 = 136. 3. number of electrons = 86.

(b) The equation is: 22286Rn → 21884Po + 42α.

(c) 7.6 days is two half-lives (7.6 / 3.8 = 2). After two half-lives, the number of radon nuclei remaining is 6.4 × 106 / 4 = 1.6 × 106. The number of nuclei that have decayed (and therefore the number of α-particles emitted) is the initial number minus the final number: 6.4 × 106 - 1.6 × 106 = 4.8 × 106.

Question 8 (0625/42_Summer_2018_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) A radioactive nucleus of uranium-235 decays to a nucleus of thorium and emits an α-particle. Complete the equation. [2]

23592U → ...Th + 42α

(b) A nucleus of uranium-235 undergoes nuclear fission in a reactor.

(i) State what is meant by nuclear fission. [1]

(ii) Suggest why a nuclear reactor is surrounded by thick concrete walls. [2]

(iii) State one environmental advantage and one environmental disadvantage of using a fission reactor to generate electrical energy in a power station. [2]

(c) The thorium produced by the decay in (a) is also radioactive and has a half-life of 26 hours. At a certain time, a pure sample of this isotope initially contains 4.8 × 109 atoms. Calculate the number of atoms of this sample that decay in the following 52 hours. [3]

(a) The completed equation is: 23592U → 23190Th + 42α.

(b)(i) Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two (or more) smaller nuclei, releasing energy.

(b)(ii) The thick concrete walls act as shielding to absorb the dangerous ionising radiation produced during fission, protecting the workers and the environment.

(b)(iii) Advantage: It does not produce greenhouse gases like CO₂. Disadvantage: It produces highly radioactive nuclear waste which is difficult and expensive to store safely.

(c) 52 hours is two half-lives (52 / 26 = 2). After two half-lives, 1/4 of the atoms will remain. The fraction that has decayed is 3/4. The number of atoms that have decayed is (3/4) × 4.8 × 109 = 3.6 × 109.

(b) Many schools and colleges use radioactive isotopes for teaching and research. Describe how these radioactive isotopes are handled, used and stored in a safe way. [3]

protonme

Question 18 (0625/43_Winter_2019_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) The circles shown in Fig. 11.1 represent three gold nuclei. Three α-particles are approaching the gold nuclei. On Fig. 11.1, complete the path of each α-particle. [3]

(b) A detector of radioactivity in a laboratory indicates an average of 16 counts/min when no radioactive samples are present. A radioactive sample of half-life 1.5 days is placed close to the detector, which indicates a count rate of 208 counts/min. Calculate the count rate that is indicated 6 days later. [4]

(c) The waste from nuclear power stations includes the isotopes technetium-99, tin-126 and selenium-79. These isotopes are radioactive with half-lives of many thousands of years. State three economic and environmental consequences of producing this waste. [3]

(a) The top α-particle is deflected back to the left. The middle α-particle is deflected on an upward curve. The bottom α-particle is deflected on a downward curve.

(b) Initial count rate from the source = 208 - 16 = 192 counts/min. 6 days is 4 half-lives (6 / 1.5 = 4). After 4 half-lives, the source count rate will be 192 / 16 = 12 counts/min. The final detector reading will be 12 + 16 (background) = 28 counts/min.

(c) 1. The waste must be stored securely with shielding, which is expensive. 2. Transporting the waste is also expensive and carries risk. 3. If there is an accident or leak, it can cause long-term contamination of the environment, making land uninhabitable for thousands of years.

Question 19 (0625/41_Summer_2020_Q10) - Atoms And Radioactivity

Fig. 10.1 represents a neutral atom of an isotope of element X.

(a) State one similarity between this atom and a neutral atom of a different isotope of element X. [1]

(b) The isotope of element X is radioactive. It decays to form an isotope of element Y by emitting a β-particle.

(i) Using Fig. 10.1 deduce the nuclide notation for the isotope of Y produced by this decay. [3]

(ii) β-particles ionise the air they pass through less strongly than the same number of α-particles. Suggest why this is so. [3]

(a) Both isotopes have the same number of protons (and also the same number of electrons).

(b)(i) From the diagram, the atom X has 5 protons and 7 neutrons, so it is 125X. In β-decay, a neutron becomes a proton, so Y will have 6 protons and 6 neutrons. The nuclide notation for Y is 126Y.

(b)(ii) This is because β-particles have a smaller charge (-1e) and smaller mass than α-particles (+2e). They also travel at a higher speed, meaning they spend less time near any given air molecule, reducing the probability of causing ionisation.

Question 20 (0625/42_Summer_2020_Q10) - Atoms And Radioactivity

Fig. 10.1 shows a vacuum tube with a radioactive source. The radioactive source emits α-particles, β-particles and γ-rays. There is a very strong magnetic field between the N pole and the S pole of the magnet.

(a) The lead cylinder has a narrow central hole. State and explain the effect of the lead cylinder. [2]

(b) Describe the paths of the α-particles, β-particles and γ-rays as they pass through the magnetic field. Explain your answers.

(i) α-particles [2]

(ii) β-particles [2]

(iii) γ-rays [2]

(a) The lead cylinder absorbs radiation travelling in other directions, producing a narrow, straight beam (collimating it).

(b)(i) α-particles are deflected out of the page. This is because they are positively charged, and applying Fleming's Left-Hand Rule predicts the force direction.

(b)(ii) β-particles are deflected in the opposite direction to α-particles (into the page) because they have a negative charge.

(b)(iii) γ-rays are undeflected because they are uncharged and therefore do not experience a force in a magnetic field.

Question 21 (0625/43_Summer_2020_Q10) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) A radioactive nucleus of carbon decays to a nucleus of nitrogen by emitting a particle. Complete the nuclide equation and state the name of the particle. [3]

146C → 147N + ...X

(b) A radiation detector in a laboratory records a reading of 10 counts/min. There are no radioactive samples in the laboratory.

(i) Explain why the radiation detector records a reading and suggest a possible source. [2]

(ii) Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5700 years. An archaeologist digs up some ancient wood. In the same laboratory as in (b)(i), a sample of this ancient wood gives a reading of 20 counts/min. An equivalent sample of living wood gives a reading of 80 counts/min. It is suggested that the age of the ancient sample is 11400 years. Do a calculation to check whether this suggestion is correct. [4]

(a) The equation is 146C → 147N + 0-1X. The particle X is a beta particle (or electron).

(b)(i) Explanation: The detector records a reading due to background radiation. Source: Cosmic rays or rocks/soil.

(b)(ii) The suggested age of 11400 years is two half-lives. The corrected count rate for living wood is 80 - 10 = 70 counts/min. After two half-lives, the expected count rate would be 70 / 4 = 17.5 counts/min. The expected detector reading would be 17.5 + 10 = 27.5 counts/min. The actual reading is 20 counts/min, which is lower than expected. This means more time has passed, so the age is greater than 11400 years. The suggestion is incorrect.

Question 22 (0625/41_Winter_2020_Q7) - Magnets And Currents, Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) A permanent magnet is made from only one material. Underline the material from which it is possible to make a permanent magnet. [1]

aluminium copper soft iron mercury plastic steel uranium

(b) An electron source produces a narrow beam of electrons that all travel at the same speed. The electron source is placed in a vacuum and the beam of electrons travels vertically downwards. Fig. 7.1 shows the beam of electrons before it passes between the N-pole and the S-pole of a magnet.

(i) Describe what is meant by the direction of a magnetic field. State the direction of the magnetic field between the two poles in Fig. 7.1. [1]

(ii) Describe and explain what happens to the beam of electrons in the magnetic field between the poles of the magnet in Fig. 7.1. [3]

(c) A beam consists of α-particles, β-particles and γ-rays. Explain how a uniform magnetic field may be used to separate the α-particles, the β-particles and the γ-rays. [3]

(a) The correct material is steel.

(b)(i) The direction of a magnetic field is the direction of the force on a N-pole. In Fig. 7.1, the direction is from left to right (N to S).

(b)(ii) The beam of electrons deflects. Since the current (conventional) is upwards and the field is left-to-right, using Fleming's Left-Hand rule, the force and deflection are into the page. A moving charge in a magnetic field experiences a force.

(c) When the beam passes through the magnetic field, the α-particles and β-particles are deflected in opposite directions due to their opposite charges. The γ-rays are undeflected as they have no charge, thus separating the three types of radiation.

Question 23 (0625/41_Winter_2020_Q10) - Atoms And Radioactivity

A radiation detector is placed on the bench in a laboratory. It detects a background count rate of 40 counts/minute.

(a) State what is meant by background radiation. Suggest one source for it. [2]

(b) A sample containing atoms of the radioactive isotope polonium-208 is removed from a lead container and brought close to the detector. The average count rate increases to 890 counts/minute. When two sheets of paper are inserted between the sample and the detector, the average count rate returns to 40 counts/minute. Polonium-208 is represented by the symbol 20884Po. It decays to an isotope of lead (Pb).

(i) Deduce the type of radiation emitted by polonium-208. Explain your answer. [2]

(ii) Write down the nuclide equation for the decay of polonium-208. [3]

(a) Background radiation is the ionising radiation that is always present in our environment. One source is cosmic rays from space.

(b)(i) The radiation emitted is alpha-particles. This is because the radiation was completely stopped by paper, which is a characteristic of alpha radiation.

(b)(ii) The decay is alpha decay. The equation is: 20884Po → 20482Pb + 42α.

Question 24 (0625/42_Winter_2020_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) State two differences between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. [2]

(b) Radioactive tracers emitting γ-rays can be used in medicine. The half-life of the source of these γ-rays is 6 hours.

(i) Explain why a source of γ-rays used in this way should not have a half-life shorter or longer than about 6 hours. [2]

(ii) Technetium-99 is a source of γ-rays often used as a radioactive tracer. It is produced from molybdenum-99 which emits β-particles. The symbol for technetium is Tc and the symbol for molybdenum is Mo. Complete the nuclide equation for this decay. [3]

...42Mo → ......Tc + ......β

(iii) State another use of radioactive nuclides in medicine. [1]

(a) 1. Fission is the splitting of a large nucleus, while fusion is the joining of small nuclei. 2. Fission produces long-lasting radioactive waste, while fusion produces much less.

(b)(i) A shorter half-life might mean the tracer decays too quickly before the scan is complete. A longer half-life would mean the patient remains radioactive for an unnecessarily long time, increasing their radiation dose.

(b)(ii) The completed equation is: 9942Mo → 9943Tc + 0-1β.

(b)(iii) Another use is in radiotherapy for treating cancer.

IGCSE Physics - Radioactivity (25-32)

Question 25 (0625/43_Winter_2020_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) Fig. 11.1 shows a beam of α-particles, β-particles and γ-rays directed between two metal plates P and Q. The metal plates are parallel and there is a large potential difference (p.d.) between them. Plate P is positive and plate Q is negative.

On Fig. 11.1, draw the paths of each of the radiations between the plates and after leaving the plates. Label the paths α, β and γ. [5]

(b) State and explain one practical application of γ-rays. [2]

(a) The α-particles, being positively charged, are deflected in a smooth curve towards the negative plate Q. The β-particles, being negatively charged, are deflected towards the positive plate P and are deflected more than α-particles due to their much smaller mass. The γ-rays are uncharged and pass straight through without deviation. After leaving the plates, all paths continue in a straight line.

(b) Application: Sterilisation of medical equipment. Explanation: γ-rays are highly penetrating and can kill bacteria and other microbes on the equipment, even through its packaging.

Question 26 (0625/42_Summer_2021_Q8) - Atoms And Radioactivity, Magnets And Currents

(a) Two identical radioactive sources emit α-particles and γ-rays into two vacuum tubes.

(i) Fig. 8.1 shows two electrically charged plates on either side of one of the vacuum tubes. Write the symbol α once in Table 8.1 to indicate any deflection of the α-particles. Write the symbol γ once in Table 8.1 to indicate any deflection of the γ-rays. [2]

(ii) Fig. 8.2 shows the poles of a very strong magnet on either side of the other vacuum tube. Write the symbol α once in Table 8.2 to indicate any deflection of the α-particles. Write the symbol γ once in Table 8.2 to indicate any deflection of the γ-rays. [2]

(b) Fig. 8.3 shows a simple direct current (d.c.) electric motor with a split-ring commutator.

(i) State and explain the direction of rotation of the coil as seen from point X. [3]

(ii) The coil rotates through 90° from the position shown. State what happens to the moment in this position. [1]

(iii) The coil is rotated through 180° from the position shown. By considering the forces on the coil, explain how the split-ring commutator enables the motor to turn continuously. [2]

(a)(i) In Table 8.1: α-particles are positive and are attracted to the negative plate (-2500V), so they deflect towards the bottom of the page. γ-rays are uncharged and have no deflection.

(a)(ii) In Table 8.2: Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule for the positive α-particles (current), the force is directed into the page. γ-rays are uncharged and have no deflection.

(b)(i) Direction: Clockwise. Explanation: Using Fleming's Left-Hand rule, the force on the left-hand wire is up and the force on the right-hand wire is down, creating a turning effect.

(b)(ii) In the vertical position (90° rotation), the moment becomes zero.

(b)(iii) The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn. This ensures that the force on the wire that is now on the left is always up, and the force on the wire that is now on the right is always down, allowing the coil to rotate continuously in the same direction.

Question 27 (0625/41_Summer_2021_Q9) - Atoms And Radioactivity

There are three naturally occurring isotopes of hydrogen: hydrogen-1, hydrogen-2 and hydrogen-3. The nuclide notation for hydrogen-1 is 11H.

(a) Write down the symbol, using nuclide notation, for: hydrogen-2 and hydrogen-3. [1]

(b) In a fusion reactor, a nucleus of hydrogen-2 and a nucleus of hydrogen-3 undergo fusion.

(i) State what is meant by nuclear fusion. [2]

(ii) The fusion reaction produces a free neutron and one other particle. Write down, using nuclide notation, the equation that represents this reaction. [3]

(c) Nuclear fusion in the Sun is the source of most but not all of the resources that are used to generate electrical energy on Earth. State two resources for which nuclear fusion in the Sun is not the source. [2]

(a) hydrogen-2: 21H, hydrogen-3: 31H.

(b)(i) Nuclear fusion is the process of joining together two small atomic nuclei to produce a bigger nucleus, with the release of a large amount of energy.

(b)(ii) The equation is: 21H + 31H → 42He + 10n

(c) Two non-solar energy resources are geothermal energy and nuclear fission (from uranium).

Question 28 (0625/43_Summer_2021_Q10) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) Fig. 10.1 shows a beam of radiation in a vacuum. The beam contains α-particles, β-particles and γ-rays. The beam enters a region where there is a strong, uniform magnetic field. The direction of the magnetic field is out of the page.

On Fig. 10.1, mark and label the paths through the magnetic field of:

(i) α-particles (label this path α) [1]

(ii) β-particles (label this path β) [2]

(iii) γ-rays (label this path γ). [1]

(b) Radioactive sources have many uses in medicine. State two safety precautions which hospital staff take when working with γ-ray sources. [2]

(c) The radioactive isotope iodine-131 is used as a tracer in medical diagnosis. A nucleus of iodine-131 contains 53 protons and 78 neutrons. The symbol for iodine is I.

(i) Use nuclide notation to show this isotope of iodine. [1]

(ii) Iodine-131 emits γ-radiation. It has a half-life of 8 hours. Explain why this emission and this half-life make iodine-131 a suitable material for use as a tracer in medical diagnosis. [2]

(a) The α-particles (positive) deflect in a downward curve. The β-particles (negative) deflect in the opposite direction (upward curve) and with a greater curvature due to their smaller mass. The γ-rays (neutral) pass straight through undeflected.

(b) Two precautions are: 1. Store the source in lead-lined boxes when not in use. 2. Limit the time of exposure and maintain a safe distance (or stand behind shielding).

(c)(i) The nuclide notation is: 13153I

(c)(ii) It is suitable because γ-rays can penetrate body tissues and be detected outside the body. The half-life is long enough for the diagnostic procedure but short enough that the patient's radioactivity decays quickly to a safe level, and it is weakly ionising.

Question 29 (0625/42_Summer_2021_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) A student investigates a radioactive substance in a laboratory. Fig. 11.1 is a graph showing the count rate detected as the substance decays for 7.5 minutes.

The background radiation is 20 counts/min.

(i) Determine the half-life of the substance. [3]

(ii) Calculate the count rate detected at time = 9.6 minutes. [2]

(b) The substance emits α-particles and γ-rays. The student suggests that it is safe to store the substance in a plastic container of thickness 2 mm. State and explain whether the student's suggestion is correct. [3]

(a)(i) The initial total count rate is 220 counts/min. Subtracting the background (20 counts/min) gives an initial source count rate of 200 counts/min. After one half-life, the source count rate will be 100 counts/min. The total detected rate would be 100 + 20 = 120 counts/min. Reading from the graph, the time taken to reach 120 counts/min is 2.4 min.

(a)(ii) The time elapsed is 9.6 minutes. The number of half-lives is 9.6 / 2.4 = 4. The source's count rate after 4 half-lives will be 200 / 24 = 200 / 16 = 12.5 counts/min. The total detected count rate will be the source rate plus the background rate: 12.5 + 20 = 32.5 counts/min (or 32/33).

(b) Statement: The suggestion is incorrect. Explanation: While the 2 mm plastic container will absorb the α-particles, it will not stop the highly penetrating γ-rays, which will pass through the container and still be dangerous.

Question 30 (0625/41_Winter_2021_Q9) - Atoms And Radioactivity

Uranium-235 (235U) is a radioactive isotope of uranium that occurs naturally on Earth.

(a) Describe the composition and structure of a neutral atom of uranium-235. [4]

(b) Another isotope of uranium is uranium-238. Describe how an atom of uranium-238 differs from an atom of uranium-235. [1]

(c) In the reactor in a nuclear power station, a nucleus of uranium-235 absorbs a slow-moving neutron and then undergoes nuclear fission. Two neutrons, a nucleus of xenon-140 (14054Xe) and a nucleus of an element represented by E are produced. Complete the equation for this fission reaction. [2]

10n + 23592U → ......E + 14054Xe + 2 10n

(d) Xenon-140 is radioactive. It decays by β-emission to isotope Q. Determine: (i) the proton number of Q, (ii) the nucleon number of Q. [2]

(a) A neutral atom of uranium-235 has a very small, dense nucleus containing 92 protons and (235 - 92) = 143 neutrons. This nucleus is surrounded by 92 electrons orbiting in shells.

(b) An atom of uranium-238 has three more neutrons (146) in its nucleus than an atom of uranium-235.

(c) To balance the equation: Nucleon number of E = (1 + 235) - (140 + 2*1) = 94. Proton number of E = 92 - 54 = 38. The element E is 9438Sr.

(d) Xenon-140 (14054Xe) undergoes β-emission. The proton number increases by 1 and the nucleon number stays the same. (i) The proton number of Q is 55. (ii) The nucleon number of Q is 140.

...U → ...Th + ...α

(a)(i) The source is background radiation (e.g., from cosmic rays or building materials).

(b) The uranium isotope is 23892U. The completed equation is: 23892U → 23490Th + 42α

(c) The mass of the isotope reduces from 16 mg to 2 mg. This reduction sequence is 16 → 8 → 4 → 2, which represents 3 half-lives. The total time taken is 3 × 3.8 days = 11.4 days.

Question 36 (0625/41_Summer_2023_Q9) - Atoms And Radioactivity

Fig. 9.1 represents all the particles in a neutral atom of a radioactive isotope X1.

(a) Determine the number of neutrons in this atom and explain how the answer is obtained. [2]

(b) The isotope X1 is a beta emitter that decays to the stable isotope X2.

(i) Describe how a nucleus of X2 differs from a nucleus of X1. [2]

(ii) Suggest why isotope X2 is stable whereas X1 is not stable. [1]

(c) The half-life of X1 is approximately 20 ms.

(i) Define the term half-life. [2]

(ii) Suggest one reason why isotopes with very short half-lives are especially hazardous. [1]

(a) Number of neutrons = 7. Explanation: The nucleus contains 12 particles (nucleons) in total. 5 of these are protons (e.g., white circles), so the number of neutrons is the total number of nucleons minus the number of protons (12 - 5 = 7).

(b)(i) In beta decay, a neutron changes into a proton. Therefore, a nucleus of X2 has one more proton and one fewer neutron than a nucleus of X1.

(b)(ii) Isotope X2 is stable because it has a more stable ratio of neutrons to protons than X1, which has an excess of neutrons.

(c)(i) Half-life is the average time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei in a sample (or the rate of decay) to halve.

(c)(ii) They are hazardous because they have a very high initial activity (rate of decay), releasing a large amount of radiation in a short time.

type of radiationnumber of protonsnumber of neutronscharge/Cstopped by

Question 38 (0625/43_Summer_2023_Q8) - Atoms And Radioactivity

21286Rn →

(a)(i) The neutron changes into a proton and an electron (the β-particle).

Question 39 (0625/41_Winter_2023_Q9) - Atoms And Radioactivity

Many household smoke alarms contain a sample of the radioactive isotope americium-241 (Am).

(a) Americium-241 is the isotope of the element americium that has the nucleon number (mass number) 241.

(i) State how the composition of a nucleus of americium-241 differs from that of a nucleus of americium-242. [1]

(ii) An atom of a different element has a nucleon number of 241. State two differences between the composition of a nucleus of this atom and a nucleus of americium-241. [2]

(b) Americium-241 decays to an isotope of neptunium (Np) by alpha-particle (α-particle) emission.

(i) Complete the equation for this decay. [3]

241...Am → ...93Np + ......α

(ii) Explain why α-particles are more strongly ionising than β-particles. [2]

(iii) The isotope of neptunium produced by americium-241 is also radioactive. The half-life of neptunium is longer than two million years. Using this information, explain the advantage of this long half-life for the use and safe disposal of a household smoke alarm. [2]

(a)(i) A nucleus of americium-241 has one fewer neutron than a nucleus of americium-242.

(a)(ii) It would have a different number of protons and a different number of neutrons.

(b)(i) The completed equation is: 24195Am → 23793Np + 42α.

(b)(ii) α-particles are more strongly ionising because they have a larger charge (+2e compared to -1e for β-particles) and they have a larger mass.

(b)(iii) The very long half-life means the neptunium decays extremely slowly, so its activity is very low. This makes the smoke alarm safe during its operational lifetime and means it does not pose a significant radioactive hazard upon disposal, making it cheap/easy.

Question 40 (0625/42_Winter_2023_Q8) - Atoms And Radioactivity

The isotope uranium-235 is represented by 23592U.

(a) State what the numbers 92 and 235 represent in this symbol. [2]

(b) Uranium-235 is a fuel used in nuclear reactors.

(i) State the process by which energy is released from uranium-235 in a nuclear reactor. [1]

(ii) A nuclide equation for this process is 23592U + 10n → 14054Xe + 9438Sr + 2 10n. Describe the mass and energy changes that take place during this process in a nuclear reactor. [2]

(c) (i) Describe how thermal energy from nuclear reactions is used to generate electricity in a power station. [3]

(ii) State one advantage and one disadvantage of using nuclear fuels in a power station instead of using fossil fuels. [2]

(a) 92 is the proton number (or atomic number). 235 is the nucleon number (or mass number).

(b)(i) The process is nuclear fission.

(b)(ii) The total mass of the products is slightly less than the mass of the initial nucleus and neutron. This missing mass is converted into a large amount of energy (thermal and kinetic).

(c)(i) The thermal energy is used to boil water to create high-pressure steam. This steam then turns a turbine, which is connected to a generator that produces electricity.

(c)(ii) Advantage: It produces no greenhouse gases. Disadvantage: It produces dangerous radioactive waste that is difficult to store safely.

Question 41 (0625/43_Winter_2023_Q9) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) For each application of radioactive isotopes, state and explain which type of radioactive emission is suitable and suggest an appropriate half-life for the isotope.

(i) household smoke alarm [3]

(ii) measuring the thickness of aluminium strips produced in a factory [3]

(b) Lead-208 (208Pb) has the highest nucleon number of the stable isotopes of lead. Explain why lead-214 (214Pb) is radioactive. [2]

(c) State two different sources of background radiation. [2]

(a)(i) Household smoke alarm: The type of emission is alpha. This is because it is highly ionising and not very penetrating. The half-life should be long (e.g., hundreds of years) so the alarm functions for many years.

(a)(ii) Measuring thickness: The type of emission is beta. This is because its penetration is sensitive to changes in the thickness of aluminium. The half-life should be long so the equipment gives consistent readings over many years.

(b) Lead-214 is radioactive because its nucleus contains too many neutrons for the number of protons, making it unstable. It will decay to reduce the number of neutrons and reach a more stable configuration.

(c) Two sources are rocks and buildings and radon gas (in the air).

Question 9 (0625/43_Summer_2018_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(ii) the nucleon number of a nuclide to decrease by 4, [1]

(iii) no change in the proton number and no change in the nucleon number of a nuclide. [1]

(i) Fig. 11.1 shows a beam of α-particles entering the electric field between two charged plates. On Fig. 11.1, sketch the path that the beam of α-particles follows in the electric field. [1]

(ii) The half-life of radon-220 is 56 s. A sample of this isotope contains 7.2 × 106 atoms. Predict the number of α-particles that the radon-220 in the sample emits in the next 168 s. [3]

(a)(i) This is caused by β-particle emission.

(a)(ii) This is caused by α-particle emission.

(a)(iii) This is caused by γ-ray emission.

(b)(i) The positively charged α-particles will be repelled by the positive plate and attracted to the negative plate, following a downward curve.

(b)(ii) 168 s is three half-lives (168 / 56 = 3). After 3 half-lives, the number of atoms remaining is 7.2 × 106 / 8 = 0.9 × 106. The number of atoms that have decayed (and α-particles emitted) is 7.2 × 106 - 0.9 × 106 = 6.3 × 106.

Question 10 (0625/42_Winter_2018_Q10) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) A detector of ionising radiation measures the background count rate in a classroom where there are no radioactive samples present. The readings, in counts/minute, taken over a period of time are shown in Table 10.1.

(i) State two possible sources of this background radiation. [2]

(ii) Explain why the readings are not the same. [1]

(b) With no radioactive sample present, a scientist records a background radiation count of 40 counts/minute. He brings a radioactive sample close to the detector. The count rate increases to 200 counts/minute. After 24 days the count rate is 50 counts/minute. Calculate the half-life of the radioactive sample. [4]

(c) Draw a line between each type of ionising radiation and its property and another line between the property and its use. One has been done for you. [3]

(a)(i) Two sources are cosmic rays from space and radioactive rocks/soil/buildings.

(a)(ii) The readings vary because radioactive decay is a random process.

(b) Corrected initial count rate = 200 - 40 = 160. Corrected final count rate = 50 - 40 = 10. The count rate has dropped from 160 to 10, a factor of 16. Since 24 = 16, this represents 4 half-lives. The total time is 24 days, so the half-life is 24 / 4 = 6 days.

(c) Matching lines: α-particle → It is the most ionising radiation... → Detecting smoke in a fire alarm system. β-particle → Penetration is affected by small changes in the amount of solid... → [No matching use given]. γ-ray → It is highly penetrating... → Remotely detecting leaks in underground water pipes. X-ray → Can pass easily through soft living tissue... → Detecting fractures in bones.

Question 11 (0625/43_Winter_2018_Q10) - Atoms And Radioactivity

Thorium-234 (234Th) is radioactive. It decays by β-emission to form an isotope of protactinium (Pa).

(a) Complete the nuclide equation for this decay. [2]

23490Th → ...Pa + ...β

(b) A pure sample of thorium-234 emits β-particles at a count rate of 2480 counts/second. The half-life of thorium-234 is 24 days. Calculate the count rate for the emission of β-particles from the thorium in the sample after 72 days have passed. [3]

(c) The isotope of protactinium in (a) is also radioactive. It decays by β-emission and has a half-life of 70 seconds. State and explain how this would affect the observed count rate for the sample in (b) after 72 days. [3]

(a) The completed equation is: 23490Th → 23491Pa + 0-1β.

(b) 72 days is three half-lives (72 / 24 = 3). The count rate after 3 half-lives will be 2480 / 23 = 2480 / 8 = 310 counts/second.

(c) The observed count rate would be larger than 310 counts/second. This is because the protactinium that is formed is also radioactive and emits its own β-particles, which would be detected in addition to those from the thorium.

Question 12 (0625/41_Winter_2018_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) Fig. 11.1 shows data about nine elements. Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope with a nucleon number of 14. It decays by emitting β-particles. Use any data you need from Fig. 11.1 to write down the nuclide equation for this decay. [4]

(b) A radioactive sample is placed close to a detector. The radioactive isotope in the sample has a long half-life. The detector records a count rate of 597 counts/s. Fig. 11.2 shows the readings when different materials are placed between the radioactive sample and the detector. Explain whether any α-particles, β-particles or γ-rays are emitted by the radioactive sample. [3]

(a) From Fig 11.1, Carbon (C) has proton number 6. Beta decay increases the proton number by 1 to 7, which is Nitrogen (N). The equation is: 146C → 147N + 0-1β.

(b) α-particles: No. If they were present, the count rate would decrease significantly with paper, but it increases slightly (within random variation). β-particles: No. If they were present, the count rate would decrease significantly with aluminium, but it barely changes. γ-rays: Yes. The count rate is only reduced significantly by the lead, which shows a highly penetrating radiation is present.

Question 13 (0625/41_Summer_2019_Q9) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) Fig. 9.1 shows a beam of α-particles moving towards a thin sheet of gold in a vacuum. Detectors in the region surrounding the thin gold sheet detect the α-particles and determine the number of particles that travel in various directions. State and explain what can be deduced from the following observations.

(i) The majority of the α-particles pass through the gold sheet undeflected. [2]

(ii) A small number of α-particles are deflected as they pass through the gold sheet. [2]

(iii) A very small number of α-particles are deflected through very large angles or return back the way they came. [2]

(b) A beam that consists of both α-particles and β-particles is passed through a region of space where there is a magnetic field perpendicular to the direction of the beam. State two ways in which the deflection of the α-particles differs from that of the β-particles. [2]

(a)(i) Deduction: Most of the atom is empty space. Explanation: Very few α-particles pass close enough to a nucleus to be affected by its force.

(a)(ii) Deduction: The nucleus is positively charged. Explanation: The positive α-particles experience a force of repulsion from the positive nucleus.

(a)(iii) Deduction: The nucleus is very dense and massive (contains most of the atom's mass). Explanation: Only a very dense, massive object could cause such a large change in momentum of the α-particle.

(b) 1. The α-particles and β-particles are deflected in opposite directions because they have opposite charges. 2. The β-particles are deflected much more than the α-particles because they have a much smaller mass.

Question 14 (0625/42_Summer_2019_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) A radon-222 nucleus contains 86 protons and 136 neutrons. It decays by emitting an α-particle and becomes a nucleus of an isotope of polonium. The symbol for radon is Rn and the symbol for polonium is Po. Write down the nuclide equation for this decay. [3]

(b) Carbon-14 is radioactive with a half-life of 5700 years. An animal bone is dug up in an archaeological excavation. The quantity of carbon-14 in the bone is 25% of what it was when the bone was buried. Calculate the time that has elapsed since it was buried. [2]

(a) The completed equation is: 22286Rn → 21884Po + 42α.

(b) A quantity of 25% remaining means the sample has undergone two half-lives (100% → 50% → 25%). The correct calculation for the time elapsed is 2 × 5700 years = 11,400 years. The official mark scheme states 11,000 years, which is likely an approximation or error.

Question 15 (0625/43_Summer_2019_Q11) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) Americium (Am) is a radioactive isotope. A nucleus of americium contains 95 protons and 146 neutrons. It decays by emitting an α-particle to form a nucleus of an isotope of neptunium (Np). Write down the nuclide equation for the decay of americium to neptunium. [4]

(b) Ionisation smoke detectors contain americium and two small electrodes with a small voltage between them. The air between the electrodes is ionised by α-particles so that there is a small electric current between the electrodes.

(i) Suggest and explain the effect of smoke on the current between the electrodes in the smoke detector. [1]

(ii) Suggest two reasons for using an α-particle emitter in a smoke detector. [2]

(a) The americium isotope is 24195Am. The equation is: 24195Am → 23793Np + 42α.

(b)(i) Suggestion: The current decreases. Explanation: Smoke particles will absorb the α-particles, reducing the ionisation of the air and therefore reducing the flow of charge (current).

(b)(ii) Reason 1: α-particles are highly ionising, which is needed to create a sufficient current in the air gap. Reason 2: They have a short range in air and are stopped by the plastic casing, making them safe to use in a home appliance.

Question 16 (0625/41_Winter_2019_Q9) - Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) The chemical symbol of the element lithium is Li. The proton number of lithium is 3. Fig. 9.1 is a representation of a nucleus of a radioactive isotope of lithium that is about to decay.

(i) Write down, using nuclide notation, the symbol that represents this isotope of lithium. [1]

(ii) This isotope of lithium decays by β-particle emission to form another nucleus. Complete Fig. 9.2 to represent this decay by: drawing a diagram of the nucleus formed by the decay, and writing the name of the particle that is identical to a β-particle. [3]

(b) A radiation detector is set up in a laboratory where there are no radioactive samples. On six separate occasions, the detector is switched on for 1.0 minute and the background count is recorded. The counts are: 23, 27, 25, 24, 20, 25.

(i) State why the readings are not all identical. [1]

(ii) Suggest a possible source for this background radiation. [1]

(iii) A sample containing only one radioactive isotope is brought into the laboratory. The half-life of the isotope is 15 hours. The sample is placed near to the radiation detector in this laboratory. The detector is switched on and, after 1.0 minute, a count of 440 is recorded. The sample is left next to the detector and the experiment is repeated 45 hours later. Predict the reading for the count obtained on this occasion. [4]

(a)(i) The diagram shows 3 protons and 5 neutrons. The symbol is 83Li.

(a)(ii) In β-decay, a neutron becomes a proton. The new nucleus will have 4 protons and 4 neutrons. The particle emitted is an electron.

(b)(i) The readings are not identical because radioactive decay is a random process.

(b)(ii) A possible source is radon gas in the air.

(b)(iii) The average background count is about 24. The initial corrected count rate is 440 - 24 = 416. 45 hours is three half-lives (45 / 15 = 3). After 3 half-lives, the sample count rate will be 416 / 8 = 52. The predicted detector reading is 52 + 24 = 76 counts.
